area: Area IV. Preflight Lesson on a Maneuver to be Performed in Flight
objective: By the end of this lesson you can build and deliver a preflight ground lesson on any maneuver the evaluator picks from Areas VII to XII: state its purpose, break it into elements with their common errors, set the desired outcome and completion standards, brief its risks, and teach it with a lesson plan, fitting teaching methods and aids.
why: On the CFI practical test the evaluator picks a maneuver, asks you to present the preflight lesson as you would teach it to a learner, and decides this Task before the flight portion (ACS AI.IV.A note). In everyday instruction the same briefing is the explanation phase of the demonstration-performance method, done before the flight lesson [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. An unprepared learner is a serious hazard, and a thorough briefing before each training flight is one of the mitigations the AIH names [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

prereading.what: How objectives give you the elements, schedule, equipment, actions and completion standards; presenting a lesson; introduction, development and conclusion.
prereading.label: AIH 5-7 to 5-10

prereading.what: Lesson plans: purpose, characteristics, how to use them, formats, the traditional plan (Figure 7-6) and the SBT plan (Figure 7-7).
prereading.label: AIH 7-7 to 7-12

prereading.what: Explanation phase, telling-and-doing, exchange of controls, distractions, integrated instruction, see and avoid, assessing elements and correcting errors.
prereading.label: AIH 9-5 to 9-12

prereading.what: Teaching risk management, TEAM, and managing the risks unique to flight instruction while teaching maneuvers.
prereading.label: AIH 10-1 to 10-8

prereading.what: Likelihood, severity, the risk assessment matrix and the three matrix errors.
prereading.label: RMH 4-1 to 4-2

prereading.what: Worked example 1: slow flight purpose, aerodynamics, procedure and the 10 common errors.
prereading.label: AFH 5-9 to 5-12

prereading.what: Worked example 2: ground reference maneuvers, wind drift and the rectangular course with its 9 common errors.
prereading.label: AFH 7-1 to 7-7

warmup: Think first: the evaluator says, "Your learner has 10 hours and has never done slow flight. Brief me as if I were that learner." You have a marker board, a model airplane and your lesson plan. What do you say in the first two minutes, what do you draw, and how will the learner know after the flight whether they did well?

key_terms.def: The ground lesson the evaluator asks for in Area IV, on a maneuver Task picked from Areas VII to XII, presented as you would teach a learner; your own previously developed lesson plans may be used (ACS AI.IV.A).
A written outline for one instructional period that tells what to do, in what order and with what procedure; another instructor should be able to teach from it [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].
The first phase of demonstration-performance, done before the flight: objectives, completion standards, a thorough preflight briefing, safety procedures and questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
The parts a maneuver is built from. Assessment must consider mastery of the elements, not just the overall performance [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
The order and timing of the lesson's activities; the components of a good objective help set it [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].
The criteria that show the objective was met; listing the objective's criteria already establishes them [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].
When learning one skill helps learning another, such as slow flight helping short-field landings [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].
What is learned first often creates a strong, almost unshakable impression, so teach it right the first time [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].
Below L/DMAX the airspeed keeps decaying after a disturbance unless the pilot lowers the AOA or adds power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
The angle the airplane is turned into the wind to cancel drift and hold a straight ground track [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
A table that combines likelihood and severity into a composite risk: high, serious, medium or low [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].
Transfer, eliminate, accept and mitigate: the steps pilots use to deal with risk [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

f1.caption: Figure 7-6. Example of a traditional training lesson plan. (AIH 7-10)
f1.alt: A sample lesson plan titled Traditional Lesson Plan. Lesson objective: the learner will learn to control for wind drift. Completion standards: consistently control for wind drift within a specified limit of heading, altitude and airspeed. Content: preflight discussion, review of heading, speed, angle of bank, altitude, terrain and wind, an introduction with turns around a point and S-turns, and a postflight discussion with critique, preview and study assignment.

f2.caption: Figure 7-7. SBT lesson plan (top part: type of training, objective, scenario, completion standards and possible hazards). (AIH 7-12)
f2.alt: Top part of a scenario-based training lesson plan. Type of training: initial. Objective: plan for arrival at a specific nontowered airport. Scenario: fly to Enterprise Municipal Airport to visit a museum. Completion standards: the learner can explain the safe arrival at any nontowered airport in any wind condition. Possible hazards: ground-based obstructions, wind, visibility and ceiling, engine-out procedures and airport traffic.

f3.caption: Figure 5-7. Slow flight: low airspeed, high angle of attack, high power, and constant altitude. (AFH 5-11)
f3.alt: A high-wing trainer flying level with its nose high. Text reads: low airspeed, high angle of attack, high power setting, and constant altitude.

f4.caption: Figure 7-4. Rectangular course. (AFH 7-6)
f4.alt: A rectangular field seen from above with the wind blowing from right to left. An airplane enters at 45 degrees to the downwind leg and flies downwind, base, upwind and crosswind legs around the field, crabbing into the wind on the base and crosswind legs, with dotted tracks showing where it would drift with no wind correction.

f5.caption: Figure 4-1. Risk Assessment Matrix. (RMH 4-2)
f5.alt: A grid with likelihood rows (probable, occasional, remote, improbable) and severity columns (catastrophic, critical, marginal, negligible). High fills probable-catastrophic, probable-critical and occasional-catastrophic. Serious fills probable-marginal, occasional-critical and remote-catastrophic. Medium covers the remaining green cells, and low is the white cells toward negligible.

f6.caption: Figure 5-6. Guidelines for presenting lessons. (AIH 5-8)
f6.alt: Three checklists. Before the lesson: decide the topic, set the time, write an outline, develop a flow, avoid overloading, rehearse. During the lesson: grab attention, make goals explicit, plan an activity, progress from introduction to conclusion, give learners time to answer. After the lesson: plan an ending, summarize, leave time for questions, critique the lesson.

f7.caption: Figure 6-4. Rubric for assessing flight training maneuvers. (AIH 6-7)
f7.alt: A rubric with four levels. Describe: the pilot can describe the physical characteristics and cognitive elements of the maneuver. Explain: can explain the underlying concepts, principles and procedures. Practice: can plan and execute with coaching and assistance. Perform: can plan and execute to ACS standards without assistance and corrects own errors. Rows list steep turns, slow flight, stalls and emergencies.

chunks.title: Area IV: what the evaluator asks for

body.p: Area IV has one Task. The evaluator selects a maneuver Task from Areas VII through XII (for a single-engine airplane) and asks you to present a preflight lesson on it, the way you would teach it to a learner. The outcome of this Task is decided before the flight portion of the test, and you may use previously developed lesson plans from your own library (ACS AI.IV.A objective and note).

head: ACS element
What it asks for
Where this lesson teaches it
rows: Elements of the maneuver and the associated common errors
Identify and manage the risk of the selected maneuver Task
Deliver instruction with a lesson plan, teaching methods and teaching aids that bring in K1 to K3

body.p: In flight-instruction terms, this Task is the explanation phase of demonstration-performance. It happens before the flight lesson and covers the lesson objectives and completion standards, a thorough preflight briefing, the precise actions the learner will perform, the end result, safety procedures, and an invitation to ask questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

The evaluator judges teaching ability by your use of the fundamentals of instructing, your knowledge of and ability to teach the maneuver, and your ability to analyze and correct common errors (ACS Appendix 1). Commercially developed lesson plans are acceptable for flight instructor applicants on the practical test, but even well-designed preprinted plans may need to be changed for a specific learner [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

callout.text: Any maneuver Task in Areas VII to XII can be picked, so build one lesson plan for each before the test, all in the same format. Then the structure is automatic on test day and your effort goes into the content (application).

check.q: When is the outcome of the Area IV Task decided, and may you bring your own lesson plans?
check.a: Before the flight portion of the practical test, and yes: previously developed lesson plans from your library may be used (ACS AI.IV.A note). Commercial plans are acceptable too, adapted as needed [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

chunks.title: From objective to lesson plan: the parts of a maneuver briefing

body.p: A good objective does much of the planning for you. The AIH says its components can be used to set the elements of the lesson and the schedule of events; the equipment needed and the instructor and learner actions are also specified; and once you list the objective's criteria, you have the completion standards [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. Every lesson plan format includes objectives, content to support them, and completion standards, but the names vary: completion standards may be called assessment, review and feedback, or performance evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

head: Part of the plan
What goes in it for a maneuver
Source
rows: What the learner will do, under what conditions, and how well
The parts of the maneuver in the order they are flown, each with its common errors
Order and time for the ground brief, the flight segments and the postflight
The airplane and its POH/AFM, aids such as a model or marker board, references
Prepare, talk through the steps, perform, self-assess
The criteria from the objective, set for this learner's stage
SBT plans list possible hazards and a mitigating strategy for each

body.p: The traditional plan in Figure 7-6 is built around one maneuver: review, explanation, demonstration and repeated practice until the learner flies it within set limits of heading, altitude and airspeed. At the end of that lesson the learner can only practice the maneuver with the instructor's help [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

The SBT plan adds a type of training, a scenario, possible hazards with mitigation strategies, and a postflight review that usually starts with the learner's self-critique [[25:156|AIH 7-12]]. SBT does not replace maneuver training: maneuvers that need repetition are still taught in concentrated sessions, then built into realistic flights [[25:154|AIH 7-10]].

callout.text: OES-EIL-C: Objective, Elements, Schedule, Equipment, Instructor actions, Learner actions, Completion standards. Then add hazards and mitigations.

check.q: Your objective's criteria say "altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10°." Which part of the lesson plan have you just written?
check.a: The completion standards: listing the criteria for the training objective establishes them [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

chunks.title: Purpose of the maneuver: start with why

body.p: K1 is the purpose of the maneuver. In the lesson introduction this is the motivation element: specific reasons why the content is important to know or perform, which ensures readiness [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]. Each lesson should also be taught so its link to the course objectives is clear; the AIH ties short-field takeoffs and landings to both the certification and the safety objectives of the course [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

Give a real-world purpose, not "it is on the checkride." The ACS is a testing document, not a training syllabus [[24:30|AFH 1-9]], and lessons should not focus on the minimum acceptable standards for passing [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

head: Maneuver
Purpose the AFH gives
Where the skill shows up later
rows: Develop the ability to fly at low speeds and high AOA, and learn the feel, sound and visual cues of a regime with degraded control response [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]
Takeoff, departure, approach and landing are flown at reduced airspeeds [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]; slow flight practice helps a learner with short-field landings [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]
Replicate the airport traffic pattern; hold a ground track, divide attention, change bank for groundspeed and correct for drift [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]
Prepares the pilot for the traffic pattern and landing pattern practice [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]
Combine the four fundamentals into integrated skills used in everyday flying [[24:147|AFH 7-1]]
Traffic patterns and any flightpath referenced to the surface [[24:147|AFH 7-1]]

body.p: Plan for transfer on purpose: tell learners where else the skill applies and prepare them to look for other uses [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. When something is taught on the ground as theory, point out how it connects to what they will do in the air [[25:172|AIH 9-2]].

callout.text: For any maneuver the evaluator picks, read the first paragraph of its AFH section: it usually states the objective in a sentence or a short list, which is your K1 answer.

check.q: A learner asks why they must learn slow flight "when we never fly that slow." What do you answer?
check.a: We do: reduced airspeeds are normal in takeoff, departure, approach and landing [[24:114|AFH 5-9]], and slow flight skill transfers to short-field landings [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

chunks.title: Elements: break the maneuver into teachable steps

body.p: K2 starts with the elements of the maneuver. Assessment of demonstrated ability must consider the learner's mastery of the elements involved, not merely the overall performance [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Keep the scope reasonable: a person can master only a few principles or skills at a time [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

Put the elements in a teaching order. Most physical skills fit a sequential pattern, explained in the same order they are flown. When a skill builds on one already learned, go known to unknown; when you teach several skills at once, go simple to complex [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Under each main point, the smaller points should lead naturally from one to the next [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].
Worked example 1, slow flight. The AFH breaks slow flight training into these elements:

head: Element
What the learner does
rows: From cruise to approach speeds without changing altitude or heading, while increasing AOA and setting power and trim [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]
Gear and flaps extended while holding heading and altitude [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]
Turns at altitude, with more power needed during the turns [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Straight climbs and climbing turns of about 20°, power-off glides and descending turns [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]
Add power, forward pressure as speed builds, coordinated, then clean up while anticipating the AOA change [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]

body.p: Worked example 2, ground reference maneuvers. The AFH gives a building-block order: first track directly over a straight line, then a parallel path offset not more than three-fourths of a mile, then the rectangular course [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. Turns around a point are a logical extension of the rectangular course and S-turns [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. Introduce ground reference work once the pilot is proficient in the four fundamentals [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

callout.text: Make the airplane's own numbers an element. One way to find the slow flight target airspeed: slow to the stall warning in the desired configuration, lower the nose slightly to stop the warning, add power to hold altitude, and note the airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

check.q: Your learner ends a rectangular course on the right track, but every turn was started late. How do you grade it?
check.a: On the elements, not only the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Failing to execute turns with accurate timing is a listed error [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

chunks.title: Common errors: brief them before they happen

body.p: The second half of K2 is the common errors that go with each element. The AFH lists them at the end of each maneuver: ten for slow flight and nine for the rectangular course [[24:117|AFH 5-12]] [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. Teach them by element, so the learner knows what wrong looks like and you know what to watch for.

head: Element
Common error (AFH)
What to tell the learner on the ground
rows: Too little back-elevator pressure (altitude loss) or too much (a climb, then a rapid loss of airspeed) [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
As power comes back, raise the nose just enough to hold altitude; trim, or strong aft pressure makes precise control hard [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Insufficient right rudder for left yaw [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
The closer to the stall and the higher the power, the more right rudder [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Not anticipating AOA changes as flaps go out or come in [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Abruptly raising the flaps in slow flight can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Below L/DMAX pitch is the better airspeed control and power controls the path; speed keeps decaying unless you act [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]
Failure to respond to a stall warning [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
React to and correct any stall indication [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]
Not assessing wind direction; no proper wind correction angle [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]
Know the wind before entry and enter downwind [[24:151|AFH 7-5]] [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]
Slips and skids; rough control use; poor turn timing [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]
Steeper bank where groundspeed is higher; adjust the roll rate to the drift [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]
Fixation, or poor division of attention between control and orientation [[24:117|AFH 5-12]] [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]
Scan several references; fixating on one point hides the rate of closure [[24:147|AFH 7-1]]

body.p: Why brief errors before the flight: primacy means the first experience leaves a strong, almost unshakable impression [[25:64|AIH 3-13]], and faulty habits are hard to correct [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. In flight, when the learner thinks out loud you can tell whether an error comes from a misconception or from a simple lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Safety permitting, it is often better to let the learner go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Do not read the AFH list as ten unrelated items. Tie each error to the element where it happens and to its fix, or the learner hears a list instead of a lesson (application).

check.q: Why include "failure to anticipate changes in AOA as flaps are extended or retracted" in a slow flight brief?
check.a: It is a listed slow flight error [[24:117|AFH 5-12]], and abruptly raising the flaps in slow flight can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

body.p: K3 is the desired outcome, including completion standards. They come from the objective's criteria [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. In authentic assessment, learners know the performance criteria before they are assessed [[25:132|AIH 6-1]], and assessment should line up with the lesson's completion standards [[25:133|AIH 6-2]].

Set them for this learner, today. Assessment must use established standards suitably modified for the learner's experience and stage [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], and lesson completion standards should gradually reach or exceed the ACS before final checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

For the rectangular course, the private and CFI ACS use the same words: enter a left or right pattern, 600 to 1,000 feet AGL at an appropriate distance from the selected reference area, 45° to the downwind leg, and maintain altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots (ACS PA.V.B.S3a and S7; AI.IX.E.S3a and S7).

Describe the outcome as a level, not only pass or fail. Learner-centered grading uses Describe, Explain, Practice, Perform and Not observed for maneuvers [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Grading is progressive: a task may be a describe item in flight one and a practice item by flight three [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

Add a decision-based outcome too. For example, before each ground reference maneuver the learner names the collision hazards and a safe emergency landing area, which the AIH suggests prompting [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. The SBT plan's completion standard is the learner explaining a safe arrival at any nontowered airport in any wind [[25:156|AIH 7-12]].

check.q: After a first slow flight lesson the learner held altitude within 150 feet, with you coaching. Was the lesson a failure?
check.a: Not necessarily. Standards are modified for the learner's stage [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], and planning and flying it with coaching that corrects deviations is the Practice level [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

chunks.title: Worked example 1: the slow flight preflight lesson

body.p: Example only (application: this lesson's own sample built from the sources, not an FAA plan). The learner is a student pilot with about 10 hours who has flown the four fundamentals.

head: Part
What you say or do
Source
rows: Ask: "On final, what happens if the airspeed decays 10 knots and nobody notices?"
Slow speeds are normal in takeoff and landing; this lesson is the base for stalls and short-field landings
Landing configuration, no stall warning; target today: Practice level, building toward private ACS altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10°, airspeed +10/-0 knots, bank ±10°
AOA and the critical AOA, controls getting "mushy," pitch for airspeed and power for path below L/DMAX, speed instability
Slow down, configure, straight and level, turns, climbs and descents, exit; one error and its fix per element
Model airplane for attitude and AOA, a sketch on the marker board, the POH for flap and gear speed limits
Demonstrate while describing, in the order you explained, then supervise
Talk you through it, then fly it while saying each step
Finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL; clearing turns; respond to any stall warning; positive exchange of controls
Retrace the elements against the objective, take questions, preview stalls, assign reading

body.p: Configuration: slow flight is typically performed and evaluated in the landing configuration, and practicing it clean or in the takeoff configuration is also good training and may be evaluated [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. The ACS says the airplane is configured as specified by the evaluator (ACS PA.VII.A.S4).

callout.text: Use the model to show the trap: if the airplane stays trimmed for cruise, strong back pressure is needed and precise control is hard [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Hold the model nose high and ask what the trim wheel should do.

check.q: Why put "pitch for airspeed, power for the path" in the slow flight brief?
check.a: Below L/DMAX small pitch changes cause large changes in induced drag and airspeed, so pitch becomes the better airspeed control and power controls the path [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

chunks.title: Worked example 2: the rectangular course preflight lesson

body.p: Example only (application). Start from something the learner knows: a boat crossing a river angles upstream to go straight across, and a slower boat or faster current needs a bigger angle [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. That is known to unknown [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

bullets: Purpose (K1): the course replicates the traffic pattern and prepares the learner for pattern and landing practice [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

Planning: pick a field with references on all four sides and fly parallel to it, outside the boundaries, one-half to three-fourths of a mile away [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. Ground reference maneuvers are generally flown 600 to 1,000 feet AGL, with at least 500 feet vertical and 2,000 feet horizontal clearance from obstructions [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Entry: downwind, so the steepest bank comes first [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]; the ACS asks for a 45° entry to the downwind leg (ACS AI.IX.E.S3a).
Roll rate: slow when the wind will drift the airplane into the course, quick when it will drift the airplane outside [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].
Errors (K2): the nine AFH errors, from clearing to turn timing [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].
Standards (K3): altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots, plus a constant track around the area (ACS PA.V.B.S4, S7).

head: Turn
Groundspeed
Bank
Turn amount
rows: More than 90°, crab toward the inside [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]
Less than 90°, crab toward the outside [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]
Medium, held, then a rapid rollout

callout.text: Keep banks at 45° or less. Flying too close to the references forces steep banks, which raise the load factor and the stall speed [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. As part of preflight planning, find the POH stall speed at 50° or the highest bank expected [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

check.q: Why does the rectangular course start on the downwind leg?
check.a: Entering downwind lets the pilot set up the steepest bank the maneuver needs first [[24:151|AFH 7-5]], and the ACS asks for a 45° entry to the downwind leg (ACS AI.IX.E.S3a).

chunks.title: Risk: what can go wrong in the maneuver you teach

body.p: R1 asks you to explain and teach how to identify and manage the risk of the selected maneuver. Risk management in flight instruction covers the dangers of maneuvers flown incorrectly by the learner close to the ground, along with every other risk of the flight [[25:185|AIH 10-1]]. Risk management belongs in all preflight and postflight briefings, and learners should lead it more as they gain experience [[25:186|AIH 10-2]].

Teach it with the tools the learner will keep using: PAVE to find hazards [[25:187|AIH 10-3]], likelihood and severity to assess them [[30:34|RMH 4-1]], the matrix to combine them [[30:35|RMH 4-2]], and TEAM to deal with them [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

head: Maneuver hazard
Why it matters
Mitigation to brief
rows: Any more AOA, load factor or less power brings a stall warning [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]
Plan to finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL and respond to every stall warning [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]
Slow flight: abrupt control or flap use
Rough inputs or abrupt flap retraction can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Smooth inputs; clean up as airspeed increases [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Less time to configure and less glide distance [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]
Have one or more emergency landing locations [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]
Towers and wires at low altitude [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]
At least 500 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from obstructions [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]
Higher load factor and stall speed [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]
No more than 45°; exit and reposition farther out if the bank gets too steep [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]
Training areas can be crowded and hazy [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]
Clearing turns; both pilots keep the lookout [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]

body.p: Assess honestly. When unsure between two levels, use the more conservative one; watch for skewing toward a lower level because you want to fly, and re-check if conditions change [[30:35|RMH 4-2]]. Medium (green) means go but still mitigate if possible; high (red) or serious (yellow) mean no-go unless mitigated [[30:35|RMH 4-2]]. In flight, you mitigate a learner's actions by operating at a safe altitude and guarding the controls, and you consciously accept the risk that remains [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

check.q: Your learner rates "engine failure during a rectangular course at 700 feet AGL" as remote and catastrophic. Where does that fall, and what mitigation do you brief?
check.a: Serious (yellow) on the matrix [[30:35|RMH 4-2]]. Brief one or more emergency landing locations before the maneuver [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

chunks.title: Risks of teaching it: safety items every maneuver brief carries

body.p: Some hazards exist only because you are teaching. The AIH lists ways to manage them: ask the learner to fly maneuvers only after appropriate training, pick practice locations with safe options, use sufficient altitude, stay alert for the unexpected, and be ready to take control [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. The learner on the controls may itself be a significant hazard, so discuss hazards in detail before and after the flight, and do not teach at the wrong time or altitude [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

bullets: Positive exchange of flight controls: brief the three-step exchange and the visual check before every flight [[24:37|AFH 1-16]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Guard the controls. Anxious learners can be very strong, and learners should never be allowed to exceed your limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

Clearing: teach one clearing procedure and insist on it before every maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. In a study of midair collisions, flight instructors were aboard in 37 percent of them [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

Distractions: most stall/spin accidents happened when attention was diverted [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]; tell the learner you will add realistic distractions, such as finding a field for a forced landing [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

Weather: if slow flight and stalls are planned on a marginal VFR day, coach the learner to see the risks, then change to the pattern, a simulation device or ground school, or reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].
External pressure: be ready to switch to classroom instruction or end a lesson early if the learner is anxious about time [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
The learner: an unprepared learner is a serious hazard; a syllabus, quality ground instruction and a thorough briefing reduce it [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

callout.text: During a takeoff the learner's attention is almost all on flying, so the AIH says to do most of the teaching before calling tower or announcing on the CTAF [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. The same idea fits every maneuver: teach on the ground, prompt briefly in the air (application).

Practice the maneuver at the altitude its source sets: slow flight completed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL in a single-engine airplane [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] (ACS AI.X.A.S2). Ground reference maneuvers should be well away from congested areas, open air assemblies of persons and livestock [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

check.q: Why does the AIH treat an unprepared learner as a hazard, and what reduces it?
check.a: An unprepared learner is a serious hazard; prudent mitigation is a syllabus, quality ground instruction and a thorough briefing before each training flight [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

chunks.title: Teaching methods and aids for a one-on-one maneuver lesson

body.p: S1 calls for a lesson plan, teaching methods and teaching aids, as appropriate. An effective instructor normally uses a combination of methods in one lesson [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. For a maneuver: demonstration-performance, with its explanation phase on the ground [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]; visualization, where the learner describes how the flight should go and you add an unexpected change and ask questions [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]; and integrated instruction, which starts with a briefing on the instrument indications as well as the outside references [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

head: Aid
Use in a maneuver brief
Source
rows: Draw the field, the wind arrow and the four turns; erase and redraw for a new wind
Show attitude, AOA and bank; easy to handle and good for questions
Handbook figures give you and the learner the same visual image
Learners see how to fly it and the performance criteria from the start
Ground instruction need not be in a classroom; the AIH example is a preflight on the actual aircraft (sitting in it to point out controls and attitudes is an application)

body.p: Choose aids for the key points: where a description would be long or complex, where you find yourself forming visual images, or where the learner is puzzled. Keep them simple with few words, and do not use them as a crutch [[25:127|AIH 5-24]]. If a two-dimensional picture does the job, use it instead of an expensive model [[25:130|AIH 5-27]].

check.q: When is an instructional aid most worth adding to a maneuver briefing?
check.a: At key points, especially when a description is long or complex, when you find yourself forming visual images, or when the learner is puzzled [[25:127|AIH 5-24]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: delivering the briefing

body.p: Organize the briefing as introduction (attention, motivation, overview), development and conclusion [[25:112|AIH 5-9]] [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. A workable order:

bullets: Attention: a story or question about the maneuver; unrelated jokes distract [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].
Motivation (K1): why this maneuver matters to this learner [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].
Overview with objective and completion standards (K3): a clear road map of what is coming [[25:112|AIH 5-9]] [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
Development (K2): the elements in the order they are flown, each with its common error; describe the end result, not just the steps [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Safety (R1): risks, clearing, altitude, exchange of controls [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Questions: invite questions on any step the learner does not understand [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

Conclusion: retrace the key elements and relate them to the objective, with no new ideas [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]; then the plan for the postflight critique, preview and study assignment [[25:154|AIH 7-10]].

body.p: Check understanding before the airplane moves. In the air, having the learner tell while you fly lets you correct a misunderstanding before the learner is busy controlling the airplane [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. On the ground, have the learner talk you through the maneuver with the model for the same reason (application).

On the checkride, teach the evaluator as your learner, as the ACS note says. Fit the plan to that learner's background, experience and ability [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Rehearse, and decide how much time the lesson takes [[25:111|AIH 5-8]]. Use simple words and avoid jargon the learner does not know [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

Brief the debrief too. After the flight the learner self-assesses with replay, reconstruct, reflect and redirect, and then you compare your assessment with theirs [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

callout.text: If the evaluator does not describe the learner, ask: hours, last lesson, what went well. The explanation phase is based on the learner's known experience and knowledge [[25:175|AIH 9-5]], so you need it to choose the starting point and the standards.

check.q: What should the overview of a maneuver briefing give the learner?
check.a: A clear, concise presentation of the objective and the key ideas: a road map of what will be covered [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

body.p: These are the errors instructor applicants make when they deliver a maneuver briefing. Each one is built from what the sources warn about.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: No purpose, or only "it is on the test"
Learner cannot say why the maneuver matters [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]
Give a real-world purpose and tie it to the course objectives [[25:153|AIH 7-9]] [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]
The ACS used as the lesson
The brief is a reading of tolerances [[24:30|AFH 1-9]]
Teach how and why; set standards that grow toward the ACS [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]
No elements, so nothing to assess piece by piece [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]
List elements in the order flown [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Learner hears a list but not what to do [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Pair each error with its element and correction [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Write criteria the learner knows in advance [[25:110|AIH 5-7]] [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]
Slow flight, stalls and spins in one brief; a confused learner [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]
No altitude, landing site or exchange of controls in the brief [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]
Brief this maneuver's hazards and mitigations [[25:186|AIH 10-2]] [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]
"Back side of the L/DMAX curve" to a 10-hour learner [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Plain words; define the term with a picture [[25:127|AIH 5-24]]
Plan not fitted to the learner
Adapt to background, experience and ability [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]
Ask for questions on every step before leaving the explanation phase [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]

callout.text: Know your plan well. A commercial plan you have not studied will show on the checkride: the AIH says to study each step of the plan and be thoroughly familiar with the subject [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

check.q: Your brief to a 10-hour learner uses "speed instability on the back side of the power curve" with no explanation. Which AIH guidance did you miss?
check.a: Avoid unnecessary jargon and technical terms the learner does not know, and describe the expected actions clearly [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

scenario.title: Area IV on the checkride: the evaluator picks the rectangular course
scenario.setup: On your CFI practical test the evaluator says: "Present the preflight lesson on ground reference maneuvers, rectangular course. I am a student pilot with 14 hours who is solid on the four fundamentals but drifts wide on downwind in the traffic pattern." The local practice area has a field bounded by roads, a 400-foot radio tower a mile east of it, and today's wind is from the west at 12 knots. You have your lesson plan, a marker board and a model airplane.

questions.q: How do you open the lesson so it meets K1?
questions.a: With attention tied to the learner's own problem, then motivation: the rectangular course replicates the traffic pattern and prepares them for pattern and landing practice [[25:112|AIH 5-9]] [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

questions.q: What order of elements do you teach, and why that order?
questions.a: Wind drift and wind correction on a straight line first, then the four legs and turns of the rectangle. Known to unknown and simple to complex [[24:151|AFH 7-5]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

questions.q: With the wind from the west, which turn needs the steepest bank if the downwind leg is flown heading east?
questions.a: The turn from downwind to base, where groundspeed is highest; it needs a relatively steep bank reduced gradually [[24:152|AFH 7-6]] [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

questions.q: What completion standard do you set for this learner today?
questions.a: A level, such as Practice: plans and flies it with coaching [[25:137|AIH 6-6]], building toward the private ACS: altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, constant track (ACS PA.V.B.S4, S7). Standards fit the learner's stage [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

questions.q: How do the tower and the low altitude change your risk brief?
questions.a: Stay at least 500 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from obstructions, have emergency landing locations, and clear the area [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Prompt the learner to name hazards and a landing site before entry [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

questions.q: The evaluator, as your learner, asks: "What if I end up too close to the field and need a really steep bank?" What do you answer?
questions.a: Exit the maneuver and re-establish a position farther from the reference; avoid banks over 45° because stall speed rises [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

skills.do: Deliver instruction on the selected maneuver using a lesson plan, teaching methods, and teaching aids, as appropriate, that incorporate K1 through K3. The evaluator sees you teach them as your learner: the purpose, the elements with their common errors, the desired outcome and completion standards, and the risks, using a written plan and at least one fitting aid, with questions invited before you finish.
skills.practice: Write one plan per maneuver Task in Areas VII to XII in the same format, then teach each to another applicant playing a learner of a stated experience level. Time yourself and ask them to grade whether they could state the purpose, the elements and the standard afterward [[25:153|AIH 7-9]] [[25:111|AIH 5-8]].

quiz.q: According to the AIH, the components of a training objective can be used to determine which two parts of a lesson plan?
options: The instructor's endorsement and the logbook entry
The elements of the lesson and the schedule of events
The aircraft rental and the fuel load
The knowledge test codes and the oral questions
quiz.why: Objective components may be used to determine the elements of the lesson and the schedule of events [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

quiz.q: At the end of the traditional lesson in Figure 7-6, what can the learner do?
options: Fly the maneuver solo to ACS standards
Practice the maneuver only with the instructor's help
Teach the maneuver to another learner
Explain a safe arrival at any nontowered airport in any wind
quiz.why: With the traditional plan the learner is only capable of practicing the maneuver with assistance from the instructor [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

quiz.q: Which part of the lesson introduction answers the ACS element "purpose of the maneuver" most directly?
options: Attention
Summary and conclusion
Overview
Motivation
quiz.why: Motivation gives specific reasons why the content is important to know, understand, apply or perform [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

quiz.q: The AIH says each lesson should be planned so its relation to the course objectives is clear. What does it relate a lesson on short-field takeoffs and landings to?
options: Both the certification and the safety objectives of the course
Only the certification objective, since the practical test covers it
Only the safety objective, since passing a test is not the real goal
Only the next lesson in the syllabus, not the course as a whole
quiz.why: Each lesson should be planned and taught so that its relation to the course objectives is clear to each learner; a lesson on short-field takeoffs and landings should be related to both the certification and safety objectives of the course [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

quiz.q: In your rectangular course brief, what does the AFH say the learner should do if a turn needs a bank that is too steep?
options: Hold the bank and add power, since 60° is acceptable for one turn
Steepen the bank further and accept some drift on the next leg instead
Exit the maneuver at once and reposition farther from the references
Keep going, but slow to below maneuvering speed first
quiz.why: Ground reference maneuvers are entered downwind so the steepest bank comes first. If the bank is too steep, the pilot should immediately exit the maneuver and re-establish a position farther from the ground reference, and banks over 45° should be avoided because of the increased stalling speed [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

quiz.q: What is the lowest altitude a single-engine slow flight practice should be completed at, per the AFH?
options: 1,000 feet AGL
2,000 feet above the terrain
1,500 feet AGL
3,000 feet AGL
quiz.why: No lower than 1,500 feet AGL for single-engine airplanes, or higher if the manufacturer recommends [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

quiz.q: In learner-centered grading, which maneuver level means the learner plans and flies it with coaching correcting the deviations?
options: Describe
Practice
Explain
Perform
quiz.why: Practice: the learner plans and executes, and coaching, instruction or assistance corrects deviations [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

quiz.q: What obstruction clearance does the AFH give for choosing a ground reference maneuver altitude?
options: At least 300 feet vertically and 1,000 feet horizontally
At least 1,000 feet vertically and 2,000 feet horizontally
At least 500 feet vertically and 2,000 feet horizontally
At least 500 feet vertically only
quiz.why: No less than 500 feet vertically above the obstruction and 2,000 feet horizontally [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

options: Teach, explain, assess, mentor
Threats, exposure, altitude, maneuvering
Transfer, eliminate, accept, mitigate
Time, energy, altitude, margin
quiz.why: TEAM represents transfer, eliminate, accept and mitigate [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

quiz.q: For the first drift-correction lesson before the rectangular course, there is no straight road or railroad near the practice area. What does the AFH suggest?
options: Choose at least three references that line up along a straight path
Skip the straight-line step and go straight to the rectangular course
Use a single distant landmark and fly toward it with no crab
Use a river's curving bank, since any shoreline gives a usable line
quiz.why: The pilot is first introduced to ground reference maneuvers by correcting for crosswind over a straight-line reference such as a road or railroad tracks. If none is available, choose multiple references (three minimum) that line up along a straight path, long enough to give time to practice [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

final_quiz.q: The evaluator picks a maneuver you did not expect. You have a commercially developed lesson plan for it. What do the sources say?
options: It is not allowed; only your own handwritten plans count
It is acceptable, but you should adapt it to the learner and know it well
It is acceptable only if the evaluator wrote it
You must teach without any plan
final_quiz.why: Commercial plans are acceptable for flight instructor applicants on the practical test, may need changes, and you should be thoroughly familiar with them [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. The ACS also allows previously developed plans from your library (ACS AI.IV.A note).

final_quiz.q: The evaluator plays a 40-hour learner who already flies slow flight well in the landing configuration. What fits the AIH best?
options: Repeat the first slow flight lesson word for word, so the plan stays standard
Teach only the aerodynamics
Skip the objective and standards
Adapt it: for example, clean and takeoff configurations and higher standards
final_quiz.why: A flight lesson plan should fit the learner's background, experience and ability [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]; slow flight in clean or takeoff configuration is good training and may be evaluated [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

final_quiz.q: You plan to give part of your slow flight brief seated in the airplane on the ramp. A colleague says real ground instruction belongs in a classroom. What does the AIH say?
options: He is right: ground instruction is most effective only in a classroom setting
He is right, unless the learner has already soloed and knows the airplane well
It need not be; the AIH example is a preflight using an actual aircraft
Use the airplane only for postflight critiques, never for the preflight brief
final_quiz.why: Ground instruction need not be in the classroom for maximum effectiveness; for example, conduct a preflight using an actual aircraft. The instructor should also point out the connection between the theory taught on the ground and the practice in the air [[25:172|AIH 9-2]].

final_quiz.q: As power comes back, your learner climbs 80 feet and then the airspeed drops quickly. Which listed error is it?
options: Excessive back-elevator pressure as power is reduced
Inadequate back-elevator pressure as power is reduced
Insufficient right rudder
Failure to clear the area
final_quiz.why: Excessive back-elevator pressure as power is reduced gives a climb followed by a rapid reduction in airspeed [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

final_quiz.q: Wind is from the west. The learner flies downwind heading east, then turns to base. What should the bank do during that turn?
options: Start shallow and steepen
Start relatively steep and be reduced gradually
Stay constant at 30°
Start at about 60° so the turn is finished quickly
final_quiz.why: Downwind to base starts with a relatively steep bank, reduced gradually as the tailwind becomes a crosswind [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]. Higher groundspeed needs a steeper bank [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

final_quiz.q: Planning the rectangular course, your learner wants to fly directly over the field's edges "to see the boundaries better." What does the AFH say?
options: Fly outside them, 1/2 to 3/4 mile away; flying close forces very steep banks
Fly directly over them, since that is the most precise way to judge the track
Fly just inside the field so the downwind turn needs only a shallow bank
Fly over them only on the downwind leg, where the groundspeed is highest
final_quiz.why: Fly parallel to the field boundaries, one-half to three-fourths of a mile away and outside them, so the references can be seen from either pilot seat. Flying directly above them is not practical, and flying close to them requires very steep banks that raise the load factor and stall speed [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

final_quiz.q: Which teaching aid does the AIH say lets learners understand from the beginning how to fly a maneuver and the performance criteria it will be judged by?
options: A cut-away model of the airplane's flight control system
A flight simulator session flown before the first lesson
A marker board sketch of the maneuver, redrawn for each new wind direction
A maneuvers guide that includes the ACS in each maneuver description
final_quiz.why: A maneuvers guide or handbook that includes the ACS as an integral part of the description of maneuvers and procedures lets learners understand from the beginning how to perform the maneuver and become familiar with the performance criteria [[25:129|AIH 5-26]].

final_quiz.q: Which completion standard best fits a learner's first rectangular course lesson?
options: "Fly a good rectangle"
No standard for an introduction
Commercial ACS standards from the first try
Plans and flies it with coaching, holding altitude about ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots, building toward the ACS
final_quiz.why: Standards are measurable [[25:110|AIH 5-7]] and modified for the learner's stage [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; ±100 feet and ±10 knots are the ACS numbers to grow toward (ACS PA.V.B.S7).

final_quiz.q: The evaluator notes your plan has no section called "completion standards," only "performance evaluation" with measurable criteria. Is that a problem?
options: No, names vary; what matters is that the plan has the standards
Yes, the FAA requires that exact heading
Yes, performance evaluation is a heading used only for written tests
No, standards are optional
final_quiz.why: All plans should include objectives, content and completion standards, and completion standards may be called assessment, review and feedback, or performance evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your practice field for ground reference work has a 300-foot tower next to it. Flying right over the tower area, what is the lowest altitude that meets the AFH vertical clearance?
options: 600 feet AGL
700 feet AGL
800 feet AGL
1,300 feet AGL
final_quiz.why: At least 500 feet above the obstruction: 300 + 500 = 800 feet AGL, inside the usual 600 to 1,000 foot range [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. The AFH pairs this with 2,000 feet of horizontal clearance, so better still, pick a reference area that keeps you 2,000 feet away from the tower.

final_quiz.q: To check your learner's thinking before the flight, you have her describe how the slow flight lesson will go, then you add an unexpected change and ask questions. What does the AIH call this?
options: Visualization
Role playing, where the learner acts out the instructor's part
Guided discussion, led by a list of lead-off questions
Telling and doing, with the learner telling while you fly
final_quiz.why: In visualization the learner describes how the flight may go under normal circumstances, the instructor adds unforeseen circumstances, and the instructor asks questions to check the learner's thought processes, without creating overburdening, unrealistic scenarios [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

final_quiz.q: During the learner's slow flight practice, how does the AIH say the instructor mitigates the risk of the learner's actions?
options: By staying off the controls entirely
By operating at a safe altitude and guarding the controls, then consciously accepting what remains
By letting the learner decide all risk
By skipping the maneuver
final_quiz.why: During flight instruction the instructor mitigates a learner's actions by operating at a safe altitude and guarding the controls, and consciously accepts the remaining risk [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

final_quiz.q: To brief wind drift for the rectangular course, you use the AFH's picture of a boat crossing a river. Which point does the analogy make?
options: A faster boat drifts farther downstream, so more speed needs more angle
Only the current's speed matters, never the speed of the boat
The boat must point straight across, and the current corrects itself
A slower boat or a faster current needs a greater angle upstream
final_quiz.why: A boat crossing a river angles upstream to counter the current and follow a straight track, and a slower boat or a faster current requires a greater angle [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Wind acts on the airplane the same way: in the AFH example a 10-knot crosswind drifts the airplane 10 NM each hour whatever its airspeed [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Starting from the familiar boat is known to unknown [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

activities.title: Fill in the slow flight lesson plan
activities.intro: Tap a part of the lesson plan, then the slow flight content that belongs in it.

pairs.r: Maneuver in the landing configuration without a stall warning
Altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10°, airspeed +10/-0 knots, bank ±10°
Model airplane, marker board and the POH flap speed limits
Explain, demonstrate while describing, then coach
Talk through each step, fly it, then self-assess
Ground brief, clearing turns, demonstration, practice, postflight

activities.title: Which AFH error list?
activities.intro: Tap an error, then the AFH list it appears on.

items.t: Insufficient right rudder to compensate for left yaw
Failure to respond to a stall warning
Failure to properly trim the airplane
Failure to properly assess wind direction
Failure to execute turns with accurate timing
Failure to establish a constant, level altitude before entry
Failure to adequately clear the area
Poor division of attention between airplane control and orientation

activities.title: True or false: outcomes and standards
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In authentic assessment, learners first learn the performance criteria after the flight.
cards.why: False. The criteria are known to learners in advance of the assessment [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

cards.s: Lesson completion standards should match the ACS from the very first lesson.
cards.why: False. They should gradually reach or exceed the ACS before final checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

cards.s: At the Perform level, the learner identifies and corrects errors and deviations without the instructor.
cards.why: True. Perform means no instructor assistance and successful completion is never in doubt [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

cards.s: Halo error is sympathy or over-identification with a learner that affects an assessment.
The CFI ACS slow flight airspeed tolerance is the same as the private ACS tolerance.
cards.why: False. Private is +10/-0 knots (ACS PA.VII.A.S5); CFI is +5/-0 knots (ACS AI.X.A.S5).

activities.title: Read the rectangular course
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin. The wind blows from right to left.

pins.label: Turn that needs the steepest bank
Crabbed toward the inside of the course
Turn that needs the shallowest bank, rolled in slowly
Crabbed toward the outside of the course

activities.title: Numbers you will brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: The airplane flies 90 knots with a 15-knot wind straight from the side. What wind correction angle holds a straight track? (angle = arcsin of crosswind / airspeed)
items.why: 15 / 90 = 0.167; arcsin 0.167 = 9.6°. The same formula gives the AFH's 12° for a 20-knot wind at 100 knots (arcsin 0.2 = 11.5°) and 6° for 10 knots (arcsin 0.1 = 5.7°) [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

items.q: Downwind at 100 knots groundspeed in a 45° bank, what is the turn radius over the ground? (radius = V squared / (g x tan bank), V in feet per second, g = 32.174)
items.why: 100 knots = 168.8 ft/s. 168.8 squared = 28,487. 28,487 / (32.174 x 1.0) = 885 feet, the AFH's "approximately 890 feet" [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

items.q: Same 885-foot radius, but upwind at 80 knots groundspeed. What bank holds it?
The airplane stalls at 48 knots at 1G. What is its stall speed in a coordinated level 60° turn (2G)?
items.why: The AFH says a 2G level turn raises the stall speed 41 percent [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. 48 x square root of 2 = 48 x 1.414 = 67.9 knots.

items.q: The evaluator specifies 57 knots for slow flight. What is the highest airspeed still within the CFI standard?
items.why: The CFI tolerance is +5/-0 knots (ACS AI.X.A.S5): 57 + 5 = 62 knots. Nothing below 57 is allowed.

activities.title: Area IV on the checkride, one decision at a time
activities.intro: The evaluator picks maneuvering during slow flight and plays a student pilot with 10 hours who has finished the four fundamentals. You have a marker board, a model airplane and your plan.

options: Start with the list of ten errors
Read the AFH slow flight section aloud
A question about airspeed on final, why slow flight matters, then an overview with the objective and standards
Ask the evaluator which elements to cover
steps.why: An introduction has attention, motivation and an overview with the objective and key ideas [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

steps.s: What completion standard do you give this learner for today?
options: Practice level, building toward the private ACS numbers
CFI tolerances
"Do your best"
None for a first lesson
steps.why: Standards are modified for the learner's stage [[25:182|AIH 9-12]] and grow toward the ACS [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]; Practice means flying it with coaching [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

steps.s: The learner asks why the nose sits so high while the power is high. Your best move?
options: Say it is just how the airplane flies
Hand them the POH
Show high AOA and low airspeed with the model, then explain why more power is needed below L/DMAX
Tell them it will make sense in the air
steps.why: Slow flight is low airspeed, high AOA and high power at constant altitude, and below L/DMAX more power is needed to fly slower [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]; a model makes the relationship visible [[25:130|AIH 5-27]].

steps.s: What goes in the risk part of the brief?
options: Nothing; the evaluator covers risk in the oral
Finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL, clearing turns, respond to any stall warning, and the exchange of controls
Only the weather
Only the ACS tolerances
steps.why: Slow flight altitude and stall-warning response [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] [[24:114|AFH 5-9]], clearing [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] and the briefed exchange of controls [[24:37|AFH 1-16]].

options: Add a quick talk on spins
Stop when time runs out
Read the error list again
Retrace the elements against the objective, invite questions and preview the flight
steps.why: A conclusion retraces key elements and relates them to the objective, with no new ideas [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]; invite questions before leaving the explanation phase [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

activities.title: Put the maneuver briefing in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the parts of the briefing in order, then tap Check.
steps: Attention: a question or story about the maneuver
Elements in the order flown, each with its common error
Risks and safety procedures, including exchange of controls

takeaways: Area IV: the evaluator picks a maneuver from Areas VII to XII; you teach the preflight lesson as to a learner, and it is graded before the flight.
A good objective gives you the elements, schedule, equipment, instructor and learner actions, and the completion standards.
K1 purpose: give the real-world reason and where the skill transfers, not "it is on the test."
K2: teach elements in the order flown, each paired with its AFH common error and the fix.
K3: measurable standards the learner knows in advance, fitted to the stage and growing toward the ACS.
R1: brief this maneuver's hazards with PAVE, the matrix and TEAM, plus altitude, clearing, landing sites and the exchange of controls.
Deliver it as introduction, development and conclusion, with simple aids, plain words and time for questions.
cfi_notes: The CFI ACS objective for slow flight says "in cruise configuration" (ACS AI.X.A objective), its S4 says "configured as specified by the evaluator," and the AFH says slow flight is typically performed and evaluated in the landing configuration [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Brief more than one configuration so the learner is ready for any of them.

The AFH target of 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] is a training aid; the ACS defines the speed by the stall warning: any more AOA, load factor or power reduction would bring one (ACS AI.X.A.S3). Teach the ACS definition and use the AFH method to find today's number.

Figure 7-6's completion standard says "within a specified limit" without numbers [[25:154|AIH 7-10]]. On the checkride, write the actual numbers and the level (Describe to Perform) you expect for the described learner.

AFH 7-5 warns about steep banks "especially in the downwind to crosswind turn" [[24:151|AFH 7-5]], but AFH 7-6 names the turn out of the downwind leg as downwind to base [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]. Teach the leg names from Figure 7-4 and the principle: the steepest bank is where groundspeed is highest.

Private, commercial and CFI slow flight tolerances differ (ACS PA.VII.A.S5, CA.VII.A.S5, AI.X.A.S5); the rectangular course numbers are the same in the private and CFI ACS (PA.V.B.S7, AI.IX.E.S7). State the standard of the certificate your described learner is working on.
If a learner cannot reach the lesson's proficiency level in the allotted time, the AIH says to schedule additional training [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Say so in your plan's completion standards section.

The AIH's takeoff guidance is to do most teaching before calling tower or the CTAF [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Applying the same idea, a thorough ground brief lets your in-flight words be short prompts (application).

Evaluators sometimes ask why you chose your aids. The AIH answer: aids go on the key points, stay simple, and a two-dimensional picture is preferred when it does the job [[25:127|AIH 5-24]] [[25:130|AIH 5-27]].
gaps: No source here sets a time limit, length or required format for the Area IV presentation; the ACS only says previously developed lesson plans may be used (ACS AI.IV.A note).
The sources do not say which maneuver Tasks evaluators pick most often, so every Task in Areas VII to XII needs a ready plan.
Slow flight speeds, flap and gear extension limits and power settings come from the POH/AFM [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
The stall speed at 50° or the highest planned bank for ground reference maneuvers must come from the POH/AFM [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
No source converts the learner-centered grading levels into ACS tolerances; deciding which numbers mean Practice versus Perform is the instructor's call.
